newsitem.title: POLAND: Rain falls, rivers rise across flood-hit Europe.
newsitem.headline: Rain falls, rivers rise across flood-hit Europe.

text.p: Heavy rain battered parts of central Europe again on Saturday and more downpours were forecast after nearly 100 people died, many bridges, roads and homes were destroyed and vast tracts of rich farmland disappeared under floodwaters.

Poland endured more rain, rivers rose and residents of some communities were told to evacuate -- but President Aleksander Kwasniewski said weather reports suggested there was no danger of a full rerun of the disastrous floods of the past two weeks.

"There is no danger of such a wave (of floods), of such water as we remember a week ago," Kwasniewski told reporters after meeting Poland's central crisis committee as new rains drenched southern and western areas just recovering from the earlier deluge.
Residents of several villages in Zielona Gora province were told to evacuate after a dyke collapsed and 20,000 troops were ordered to help shore up national communications.
Floods have killed 49 people in Poland alone, swamped 400,000 hectares (almost one million acres) of land and affected about 1,000 communities, including the towns of Wroclaw and Opole.
Flood waters meanwhile continued to advance across Austria, wrecking homes and forcing the organisers to move the opening night of Bregenz arts festival from its floating stage on Lake Constance.
The Alpine republic is suffering its worst floods this century and meteorologists hold out little hope of an early end to the precipitation in central Europe.
Rain was forecast throughout the weekend over the flatlands of the Danube basin and in the provinces of Upper Austria and Styria.
"If it carries on raining, as has been forecast, the situation will become even more critical," said Rudolf Harra, fire chief in Grieskirchen, Upper Austria.

The northern region of Upper Austria has been worst hit by the flooding. The Trattnach and Aschach rivers broke their banks on Friday and tore through the Grieskirchen area, ripping down bridges and dislodging oil storage tanks.

In the western Vorarlberg region, downpours triggered mudslides and forced the organisers of Bregenz festival to relocate the Friday evening premier. Gershwin's opera Porgy and Bess was hastily moved inside Bregenz opera house from a spectacular outdoor stage on Lake Constance.
In the southern province of Styria, fire crews were on alert in case the Enns river burst its banks.
River levels also rose steadily in the Czech Republic, particularly the Elbe amd Morava.
Roads were still blocked in the badly affected eastern region of Moravia and only one border crossing to Slovakia, at Lanzhot, was open to rail and road traffic.
Rainfall was particularly heavy -- 134 mm (5.25 inches) -- over the Krkonose mountains along the Czech-Polish frontier.
Many people in flooded areas were advised to buy dry food and bottled water because the mains water supply was feared to have been contaminated.
The Czech weather service said it expected rain and storms to continue until Tuesday.
Hungary forecast more rain in the west and showers in central areas, but the fear was that the Danube would bring in floodwaters next week from Bavaria and Austria.
In Germany, there was a sense of relief as the feared high water failed to materialise overnight and forecast was for showers rather than torrential rain.
